result.markdown: --- title: "Study design" subtitle: "Fantastic Data and Where to Find Them" author: "Yu Cheng Hsu" title-slide-attributes: data-background: /assets/images/functional-genomics/background-1.png data-background-size: 40% 100% data-background-position: right data-background-opacity: "0.8" format: revealjs: theme: [default, ../../../assets/css/general_style.css] slide-number: true smaller: true lightbox: true chalkboard: theme: whiteboard src: None lightbox: true --- ## Learning objectives - Identify different type of medical data sources - Understand the pros and cons of different medical data sources # Observational Study Designs in Health Data ## Overview of observational studies ::: {.cell} ::: The observational data study was categorized by - Unit of observation - Direction of temporal tracking. # Population Level study ## Ecological Study - Unit of observation: group or population - Data Source: Government statistics, health surveillance - Common analytical framework: Poisson/Negative binomal regression **Ecological Fallacy** - Inappropriately inferring an individual-level association from group-level aggregated data. ## Key measures in disease descriptions - **Prevalence** ≈ how common the disease is *right now* in a group $$ \text{Prevalence} = \frac{\text{Number of ALL existing cases (new + old) at a specific time}}{\text{Total population at that specific time}} $$ - **Incidence** ≈ how many *new* cases appear over a period of time $$ \text{Incidence Rate} = \frac{\text{Number of NEW cases during a specific time period}}{\text{Population at risk during that time period}} $$ ## In class activity Skim through the Journal article [The association of arsenic exposure with mortality due to cancer, diabetes, Alzheimer's and congenital anomalies using Poisson regression](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42744-4) Answer the following question: - What is the surveillance periord? 2016–2020 - What is the sample size? 8042 Deaths - What statistical methods is used Poisson regression - Is there any comparision group? No - The study claim it's an association or causation? Association - What are the outcome measures ? Incidence rate - How does the authors report the association or causation? Relative risk # Individual Level study ## Key measures in epidemiology :::{.columns} :::{.column} - **Relative risk (RR)** $$ \begin{aligned} \text{Risk} & = \frac{\text{Events}}{\text{Total Everyone}} \\ \text{RR} & = \frac{\text{Risk}_{\text{exposed}}}{\text{Risk}_{\text{unexposed}}} \end{aligned} $$ Question answered: "How many times more likely is the event in the exposed group?" ::: :::{.column} **Odds ratio (OR)** $$ \begin{aligned} \text{Odds} & = \frac{\text{Events}}{\text{Non-Events}} = \frac{p}{1 - p} \\ \text{OR} & = \frac{\text{Odds}_{\text{exposed}}}{\text{Odds}_{\text{unexposed}}} \end{aligned} $$ Question answered: "How many times higher are the odds of the event in the exposed group?" ::: ::: - Metric = 1.0: No association (exposure does not change the risk/odds). - Metric > 1.0: Harmful exposure (higher risk/odds in the exposed group). - Metric < 1.0: Protective exposure (lower risk/odds in the exposed group). ## Cohort study **Cohort** A group of people who share a common characteristic or experience within a defined period of time. **Idea** 1. Select a group of people (cohort) 1. with shared similar characteristics (Age, sex, etc.) 2. with different **exposures** (e.g., smoking vs. non-smoking) 2. Follow them over time to see who develops the disease of interest (e.g., lung cancer). - Data Source: EHR - Common analytical framework: Logistic regression, machine learning models ## Retrospective cohort study Looking back from the history of the cohort to determine exposure status and outcome. 1. Find out who were exposed and who were not exposed in the past. 2. Find out who develops the disease of interest after the exposure. ![Illustration of retrospective cohort study](/assets/images/epi1/retro_edit.png){width=65%} ## Case control study 1. We select a group of people with - similar characteristics (e.g., age, sex) - with different **disease** (e.g., cancer vs. non-cancer), 2. Check what kind of exposure they had before the disease ![Illustration of case-control study](/assets/images/epi1/case-control.png){width=65%} ## Comparison | Feature | Cohort | Case-Control | |------------------------|------------------------------|-------------------------------| | Starting Point | Exposure status | Disease status (Outcome) | | Direction of Inquiry | Forward (Exposure → Outcome) | Backward (Outcome → Exposure) | | Primary Metric | Relative Risk (RR) | Odds Ratio (OR) | | Ideal Use Case | Rare exposures | Rare diseases | | Can measure incidence? | Yes | No | # Workshop: cohort study ## Scenario: A suspected outbreak :::{.columns} :::{.column} **Presenting issue** A small community that relies on two drinking-water sources, Water Source A and Water Source B. Several residents develop disease after directly drinking water. ::: :::{.column} **Questions** Investigators want to know whether living near one water source increases the risk of infection. ::: ::: ![Illustration](/assets/images/epi_workshop/illustration.png){width=70%} ## Activity instructions In a cohort study, we follow a specific population based on their exposure status to observe their future probability of developing a disease. 1. **Everyone in the class:** show only the card back (Water Source) and hide the face. 2. **Investigation**: leave your seat and find $N$ **residents from Area A** and $N$ **residents from Area B**. 3. Once you find them, ask them to *reveal* their card faces and record whether they are infected (Red card). 4. Record your data in the table below in R: | Cohort Study | Infected (Red) | Healthy (Black) | | :--- | :---: | :---: | | **Water Source A (Exposed = $N$)** | a | b | | **Water Source B (Unexposed = $N$)** | c | d | ## Interpretation of cohort study The fundamental question we can answer is: > Compared with the **unexposed** group, how likely is the **exposed** group to develop the disease (outcome)? To answer this, we need to know 1. How likely is the outcome to occur in the unexposed group? (Risk) 2. How likely is the outcome to occur in the exposed group? (Risk) 3. Calculate the ratio of 2. to 1. (Relative Risk) --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Enter the data (a, b, c, d) you collected from your Cohort Study a <- 15 # Number of infected in Area A (example) b <- 3 # Number of healthy in Area A (example) c <- 2 # Number of infected in Area B (example) d <- 10 # Number of healthy in Area B (example) # Calculate the Risk (Incidence) risk_A <- a / (a + b) risk_B <- c / (c + d) # Calculate Relative Risk (RR) RR <- risk_A / risk_B cat("Relative Risk (RR) of the Cohort Study:", round(RR, 2), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Relative Risk (RR) of the Cohort Study: 5 ``` ::: ::: **Discussion** Current methods is the simplest way to estimate the RR. However, some obvious pitfall includes - Cannot incorporate other control variables (e.g. sex, age, etc ...) - Cannot get a confidence interval to perform inference test. ## Generalized linear model Helper function: Transform contingency table to proper long table with age as confounder ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Expand 2x2 counts into individual patient rows cohort_data <- data.frame( exposure = factor(c(rep("A", a + b), rep("B", c + d)), levels = c("B", "A")), infected = c(rep(1, a), rep(0, b), rep(1, c), rep(0, d)) ) # Simulate a confounder: older age increases both exposure to A and infection risk set.seed(42) cohort_data$age <- round(rnorm(nrow(cohort_data), mean = 45, sd = 5) + ifelse(cohort_data$exposure == "A" & cohort_data$infected == 1, 5, 0)) head(cohort_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` exposure infected age 1 A 1 57 2 A 1 47 3 A 1 52 4 A 1 53 5 A 1 52 6 A 1 49 ``` ::: ::: ## Poisson Regression (Directly Estimating RR) - Estimate Relative Risk with covariate adjustment through Poisson regression $$ \ln(P(Y = 1 \mid X)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Exposure} + \sum \beta_k X_k $$ Exponentiating $\beta_1$ yields the Relative Risk: $$ \text{RR} = e^{\beta_1} $$ ## :::{.columns} :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(sandwich) library(lmtest) # Fit Modified Poisson Model poisson_model <- glm(infected ~ exposure + age, data = cohort_data, family = poisson(link = "log")) summary(poisson_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = infected ~ exposure + age, family = poisson(link = "log"), data = cohort_data) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -3.39725 1.91028 -1.778 0.0753 . exposureA 1.35949 0.80072 1.698 0.0895 . age 0.03611 0.03929 0.919 0.3581 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1) Null deviance: 19.311 on 29 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 11.747 on 27 degrees of freedom AIC: 51.747 Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Robust Sandwich Standard Errors robust_se <- coeftest(poisson_model, vcov = vcovHC(poisson_model, type = "HC0")) # Extract adjusted RR and 95% CI rr_est <- exp(robust_se["exposureA", "Estimate"]) rr_ci <- exp(coef(poisson_model)["exposureA"] + c(-1.96, 1.96) * robust_se["exposureA", "Std. Error"]) # Printing results cat("Adjusted Relative Risk (Poisson):", round(rr_est, 2), ", 95% CI: [", round(rr_ci[1], 2), ",", round(rr_ci[2], 2), "]\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Adjusted Relative Risk (Poisson): 3.89 , 95% CI: [ 1.09 , 13.94 ] ``` ::: ::: - Poisson regression overestimates standard errors in this example (as outcome is 1 or 0) - Robust sandwich standard errors (sandwich and lmtest packages) to produce valid 95% confidence intervals. ::: ::: ## Logistic Regression (Estimating Odds Ratios) Alternative model is the logistic regression model Modle the log-odds using a logit link: $$ \ln\left(\frac{P(Y = 1)}{1 - P(Y = 1)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Exposure} + \sum \beta_k X_k $$ Exponentiating $\beta_1$ yields the Odds Ratio: $$ \text{OR} = e^{\beta_1} $$ ## ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fit Logistic Regression Model logistic_model <- glm(infected ~ exposure + age, data = cohort_data, family = binomial(link = "logit")) # Extract adjusted OR and 95% CI or_est <- exp(coef(logistic_model)["exposureA"]) or_ci <- exp(confint.default(logistic_model)["exposureA", ]) summary(logistic_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = infected ~ exposure + age, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = cohort_data) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -8.1736 4.0678 -2.009 0.04450 * exposureA 2.7570 1.0679 2.582 0.00983 ** age 0.1442 0.0846 1.704 0.08838 . --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1) Null deviance: 41.054 on 29 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 23.530 on 27 degrees of freedom AIC: 29.53 Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Adjusted Odds Ratio:", round(or_est, 2), "95% CI: [", round(or_ci[1], 2), ",", round(or_ci[2], 2), "]") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Adjusted Odds Ratio: 15.75 95% CI: [ 1.94 , 127.76 ] ``` ::: ::: ## OR v.s. RR - Historical issue: - Poisson regression does not guarntee a stable answer - Over-estimation (i.e. in our example we need additional package solving this) - Commercial softwares (SAS,SPSS) default is logistic regression Nowaday selection of using OR (logistic regression) or RR (Poisson regression) in cohort study based on the consideraion - RR-Poisson Regression: Golden standard for top-tier journals, common disease - OR-Logistic Regression: Case-control study, prediction modeling (AI) rare disease ## OR approximate to RR Let's recall the formulas using our $2 \times 2$ table counts ($a$ = Exposed Cases, $b$ = Exposed Controls, $c$ = Unexposed Cases, $d$ = Unexposed Controls). :::{.columns} :::{.column} **Relative Risk (RR):** $$ \small RR = \frac{\text{Risk in Exposed}}{\text{Risk in Unexposed}} = \frac{\frac{a}{a+b}}{\frac{c}{c+d}} $$ ::: :::{.column} **Odds Ratio (OR):** $$ \small OR = \frac{\text{Odds in Exposed}}{\text{Odds in Unexposed}} = \frac{\frac{a}{b}}{\frac{c}{d}} = \frac{a \times d}{b \times c} $$ ::: ::: If a disease is extremely rare (e.g., 1 in 10,000 people), the number of sick ($a$ and $c$) is incredibly tiny compared to the healthy people ($b$ and $d$). If $a$ is vanishingly small, then adding it to $b$ barely changes anything. Therefore the following approximation holds $$ \small \begin{aligned} a \ll b \implies & a + b \approx b \\ c \ll d \implies & c + d \approx d \end{aligned} $$ ## Summary | Context | Recommend methods | Why? | | --- | -- | ------| | **Outcome is Rare ($<5\% - 10\%$)** | **Logistic Regression** | $\text{OR} \approx \text{RR}$; computation is fast, robust, and universally accepted. | | **Outcome is Common ($>10\%$) in a Cohort** | **Poisson Regression** | Directly yields an interpretable Relative Risk without exaggerating effect size. | | **Prediction Modeling / Risk Calculators / Case control study** | **Logistic Regression** | Guaranteed to bound individual risk estimates within $[0, 1]$. |

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
